title: Kafka Streams: Dense Notes on Streams, Tables, Windows & Exactly-Once
summary: A 10-page handwritten study series covering Kafka Streams end to end: the KStream/KTable duality, state stores, windowing, stream-table joins, exactly-once semantics, repartitioning internals, operations, and the mistakes that trip people up.

chapters.title: Kafka Streams in One Page
points: Kafka Streams is a JVM client library for stream processing -- no separate compute cluster; your app's processes ARE the processors
Topology = DAG of nodes: source nodes read Kafka topics, sink nodes write back, others transform; print it with Topology.describe()
Two APIs: high-level DSL (StreamsBuilder, KStream/KTable) and low-level Processor API (process(), punctuators) -- they interoperate
StreamsConfig essentials: application.id, bootstrap.servers, default key/value serdes, processing.guarantee, num.stream.threads
application.id does triple duty: consumer group id + prefix for all internal topics (changelogs, repartition) -- never reuse across topologies
Unit of parallelism = StreamTask, one per partition of the max-partitioned input; num.stream.threads spreads tasks across threads
Scale out by adding instances -- the consumer group protocol reassigns tasks, and state follows via changelog restore
Hello world (word count): builder.stream("words").flatMapValues(split).groupBy((k,w)->w).count(Materialized.as("counts")).toStream().to("out")
Under the hood: a normal consumer reads, an idempotent-capable producer writes, group coordination handles membership -- all in one JVM
Stateless ops (map/filter/flatMap) need no storage; stateful ops (count/aggregate/reduce/join/window) create state stores
Sweet spots: real-time ETL, event-driven microservices, enrichment, fraud detection, real-time analytics on Kafka data
Not this tool: it is not SQL-on-Kafka (that is ksqlDB), not a batch engine, and does not replace your sink databases

chapters.title: KStream vs KTable: Events vs State
points: KStream = immutable event log: every record is a new fact, INSERT-only, nothing is ever overwritten
KTable = changelog view of a mutable dataset keyed by record key: new value for a key = UPDATE, null value = tombstone (DELETE)
Example: clicks stream (every click matters) vs users table (only the latest profile per user_id matters)
Semantics differ downstream: a KStream sees pre-delete events; a KTable only exposes the latest value per key at read time
Duality: a table is the snapshot of latest values; its changelog is the same data as an event stream -- toStream() and aggregation convert between them
Every KTable is backed by a compacted changelog topic; replaying it rebuilds the table -- this is how table state materializes
Conversions: KStream.toTable() builds a table; table.toStream() yields changelog records (deletes arrive as null values)
Null keys: legal on a KStream (rarely useful) but tables and grouped ops skip null-key records -- validate keying upstream
KGlobalKTable = table fully replicated to every instance; you trade memory and bandwidth for joins without co-partitioning
A KTable is a semantic type, not a queryable database -- to read it interactively, materialize it into a store with Materialized.as(...)
Rule of thumb: entity/profile/reference data -> KTable; continuous flow of events or metrics -> KStream
Both types partition by serialized key bytes (murmur2), so serde discipline matters identically for streams and tables

chapters.title: State Stores: The Engine Room
points: Stateful operators (aggregate, reduce, count, joins, windowed ops) read and write a state store scoped to their task
Store shapes: KeyValueStore, WindowStore (key + window start), SessionStore -- built via StoreBuilder or Materialized.as("name")
Engines: RocksDB (default: on-disk, off-heap, survives restarts) vs in-memory (fast, simple, capped by heap)
Durability model: every store is backed by a compacted changelog topic (application.id-name); each write goes to store + changelog
Recovery: a task that fails or moves is rebuilt by replaying the changelog with a restore consumer; standby replicas shortcut this
Changelog compaction keeps the latest value per key; windowed changelogs add segment-based TTL so expired windows are cleaned up
Record caching (statestore.cache.max.bytes, default 10 MB per task): a write-behind buffer batching changelog + downstream updates -- throughput up, freshness down
Interactive Queries: find a store by name on the local thread and read it as a ReadOnlyKeyValueStore -- your aggregates become a queryable view
IQv2 adds typed range/prefix queries; across instances you need REST endpoints + StreamsMetadata (application.server) for owner discovery
Memory gotcha: RocksDB uses OFF-heap memory (block cache, memtables, index blocks) -- JVM -Xmx says nothing about its footprint; budget container memory accordingly
Tuning knobs: state.dir on fast disk, RocksDB block cache + bloom filters, withCachingEnabled/Disabled, withLoggingEnabled(changelog configs)
Anti-pattern: treating stores as databases -- no secondary indexes, no cross-task queries; design your keys for the exact access pattern

chapters.title: Windowing: Bounding Infinite Time
points: Aggregations over infinite streams need bounded scopes -- windows slice by event time, sessions slice by inactivity gap
Tumbling windows: fixed size, aligned, non-overlapping -- each record lands in exactly one window (e.g., 1-minute error counts)
Hopping windows: fixed size + advance interval; they overlap, so one record can hit multiple windows (5-min window every 1 min)
Sliding windows (first-class since 3.0, KIP-450): fixed-duration windows that follow each record -- ideal for 'X events in the last Y minutes'
Session windows: no fixed size; a session = activity until an inactivity gap, and a late event can MERGE adjacent sessions
Event time comes from record timestamps via TimestampExtractor; stream time advances to the max timestamp a task has seen (watermark-like)
A window closes when stream time passes window end + grace period; its result lives in a window store until retention expires
Grace period (default 24h for time and session windows) admits out-of-order records; data later than end+grace is DROPPED (watch the dropped-records metric)
suppress(Suppressed.untilWindowCloses(...)) emits ONE final result per window instead of an update on every record -- cleaner downstream
Retention vs grace: retention = how long window state lives; grace = how long late data is still accepted -- grace should fit inside retention
Code sketch: .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(5), Duration.ofSeconds(30))).count()
Gotcha: windows exist per KEY -- 'per-minute counts' means per-key-per-window state, so high-cardinality keys x windows = state growth

chapters.title: Stream-Table Joins: Enrichment & Correlation
points: KStream-KTable join = enrichment: each stream event is joined against the table's LATEST value for the same key (classic orders-join-users)
Asymmetric semantics: only stream records trigger output, using current table state; table updates never emit and never retro-join old events
KStream-KStream join: windowed via JoinWindows.of(...); both sides are buffered in window stores and every pair inside the window emits (inner/left/outer)
KTable-KTable join: changelog-to-changelog join producing a new KTable -- updates on either side recompute the joined row
Foreign-key join (2.4+): table-to-table join on a key derived from the VALUE, e.g. orders.product_id -> products, not the record key
KStream-GlobalKTable join: a KeyValueMapper extracts the join key per record; no co-partitioning needed because the table is fully local
All non-global joins require co-partitioning: same partition count + same partitioner on the join key, or Streams fails fast with a TopologyException
Fixing co-partitioning: re-key and repartition one side, or pre-create topics with matching partition counts -- Streams checks, it does not fix
Cost profile: stream-table is an O(1) store lookup per event; stream-stream buffers O(window size) on both sides plus constant store churn
Join windows and grace live in real state stores, so changelog traffic, restore time and disk all scale with your window size
Null handling: null join keys never match; a tombstoned table row enriches with nulls -- pick inner vs left join by business need
Code sketch (FK join): orders.join(products, order -> order.productId(), (order, product) -> enrich(order, product))

chapters.title: Exactly-Once Processing
points: Guarantee menu: at-most-once (fast, may lose), at-least-once (default, may duplicate), exactly-once (atomic consume-transform-produce)
Enable EOS with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 (the default EOS version since 3.0; v1 is deprecated)
One EOS cycle: begin transaction -> consume offsets -> process -> write outputs + changelog updates -> sendOffsetsToTransaction -> commit, every commit.interval.ms
Atomic unit = consumed offsets + produced records + changelog updates in ONE transaction -- a crash aborts all three, so neither duplicates nor loss appear
Downstream MUST read with isolation.level=read_committed, or consumers see aborted records and phantom lag (data before the Last Stable Offset)
commit.interval.ms defaults to 100 ms under EOS vs 30 s otherwise -- smaller = lower latency but more coordinator load; larger = better throughput
Zombie fencing is built in: the transactional producer epoch makes writes from an old (zombied) generation fail after initTransactions()
EOS v2 (KIP-447): ONE transaction per instance covering all its tasks, instead of per-task transactions -- fewer transactions, higher throughput
Recovery path: task crash -> transaction aborted -> task reassigned -> state rebuilt from changelog -> processing re-runs but output becomes visible exactly once
Hard boundary: EOS covers Kafka-to-Kafka only -- external side effects (HTTP calls, DB writes) need idempotency keys or an outbox pattern
Costs: commit-interval latency, transaction coordinator load, visible lag spikes during open transactions, throughput tax on very high-volume topologies
Pragmatic alternative: at-least-once + idempotent/upsert sinks (keyed writes) often meets business needs at lower cost -- choose deliberately

chapters.title: Repartitioning & Co-Partitioning Internals
points: Rule: changing a record's key invalidates its partition assignment -- the next stateful op auto-inserts a repartition step (groupBy, re-key before join)
groupByKey reuses existing partitioning; groupBy with a new key always creates a repartition topic -- prefer groupByKey when the key is unchanged
Repartition topics are internal auto-created topics (application.id-...-repartition); tune name and partitions via Repartitioned.as("x").withNumberOfPartitions(n)
Internally the topology writes to the repartition topic via a sink node and reads it back via a source node -- visible in Topology.describe()
Co-partitioning rules for joins: identical partition counts + the same partitioning function (default murmur2 over serialized key bytes) on both sides
topology.optimization=all can eliminate redundant repartition nodes (e.g., reuse source partitioning) -- set StreamsConfig.TOPOLOGY_OPTIMIZATION
Custom partitioning via StreamPartitioner / DEFAULT_PARTITIONER_CLASS -- beware breaking murmur2 compatibility with existing topic data
Skew: hot keys overload one task (lag + unbalanced state); mitigate with salting (key#shard + two-phase aggregate) or re-keying
Data locality: a task's stores hold only its partitions -- after a rebalance, stores move and must be restored; keep key-to-task mapping stable
Re-key cost checklist: extra producer+consumer traffic, extra broker storage, an extra serde round-trip per record
Never delete internal topics while the app runs; to reprocess from scratch use kafka-streams-application-reset (wipes offsets + internal topics)
Debug tip: 'not co-partitioned' errors at startup mean partition counts or partitioners mismatch -- check partition counts and serdes first

chapters.title: Scaling, Fault Tolerance & Operations
points: Parallelism math: task count = partitions of the max-partitioned input; instances x threads beyond the task count just sit idle
num.stream.threads controls intra-instance parallelism; one thread runs many tasks, and each task owns one partition's stores
num.standby.replicas=1 mirrors each task's state on a second instance -- failover becomes a task switch instead of a full changelog replay (cost: 2x storage)
Failure flow: instance dies -> group rebalances -> tasks and their stores reassigned -> new owner restores from changelog -> resumes from last committed offsets
Cooperative-sticky rebalancing is supported (with a documented upgrade path) -- avoids stop-the-world rebalances that pause all tasks
Monitor: consumer lag (records-lag-max), process/commit latency, RocksDB block-cache hit rate and store size, restoration rate, dropped late records
Sizing state: state size is roughly keys x value size x retention; put state.dir on fast local SSD/NVMe and size disks for changelog restore bursts
RocksDB care: tune block cache and bloom filters, watch compaction (bytes-written rate) -- it is usually the disk I/O hog
Graceful shutdown: kafkaStreams.close(Duration) lets tasks commit, flush caches and close stores; kill -9 forces changelog restore on the next owner
Deployment: any scheduler works since state is restorable, but provision fast local or attached disk and a stable state.dir path
Testing: TopologyTestDriver runs your topology in-JVM without Kafka -- unit-test windows, joins and suppression with TestInputTopic/TestOutputTopic
Upgrades: rolling restarts are safe across patch versions, but changelog format or topology changes may need application-reset or dual-topic migration -- read release notes

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Gotchas
points: Using groupBy where groupByKey suffices -> a needless repartition topic and broker round-trip on every aggregation
Joining without co-partitioning -> the app crashes at startup; input topic partition counts must match on both sides
Relying on null keys: records with null keys silently vanish from tables and aggregations -- validate keying at the producer
Treating null values as 'empty data': in tables they are tombstones (deletes); a careless filter before aggregation changes delete semantics
Wrong or missing TimestampExtractor -> windows silently keyed by ingestion time; clock-skewed producers shift records into wrong windows
Leaving the 24h default grace period on high-cardinality keys -> a full day of window state and multi-GB stores; set grace explicitly
Setting grace to 0 for 'clean windows' -> legitimate late data is silently dropped; alert on the dropped-records metric
Deserialization errors kill threads by default (LogAndFail) -- attach a DeserializationExceptionHandler (log-and-skip or DLQ) on risky topics
Unbounded state: aggregating by ever-unique keys (session ids, uuids) with no retention -> changelog and RocksDB grow forever
Running exactly_once_v2 while downstream reads with read_uncommitted -> aborted records become visible duplicates
IQ misuse: querying a store on an instance that does not own the key returns nulls/empty -- discover owners via StreamsMetadata first
Reusing application.id across different topologies -> corrupted internal topics; and renaming the app resets all state (new changelog names)

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Decisions & Mental Model
points: Mental model: topics are logs, KStream is facts over time, KTable is latest-value-per-key (a materialized view), state stores are its disk
Type picker: events/metrics -> KStream; entity state -> KTable; small slow dimension for joins -> KGlobalKTable
Join picker: enrichment -> stream-table; event correlation in time -> windowed stream-stream; changelog consistency -> table-table; value-derived keys -> FK join
Window picker: periodic rollups -> tumbling; smoothed trends -> hopping; threshold-in-window alerts -> sliding; user journeys -> session
Guarantee picker: Kafka-to-Kafka and correctness-critical -> exactly_once_v2; external sinks -> at-least-once + idempotent writes
Defaults to memorize: grace 24h, commit.interval 100ms (EOS) / 30s (at-least-once), record cache 10 MB/task, RocksDB engine, 0 standby replicas
Golden APIs: StreamsBuilder, KStream (map/filter/join/aggregate), KGroupedStream, TimeWindows/SessionWindows/JoinWindows, Materialized, Suppressed, Repartitioned
Performance levers, ranked: fewer repartitions > balanced partitions (no hot keys) > cache sizing > RocksDB tuning
Correctness checklist: non-null keys, matching serdes, verified co-partitioning, validated event timestamps, deliberate grace periods
Reliability checklist: sane changelog compaction/retention, standby replicas for fast failover, DLQ exception handlers, alerts on lag and restore time
Cost checklist: state size x retention fits local disk, repartition topics kept lean, transaction interval balancing latency vs coordinator load
One-liner: Kafka Streams is a partition-parallel consume-transform-produce DAG where tables are changelogs, joins are key-parallel lookups, windows bound time, and EOS makes the whole cycle atomic
